t: What are Kronos's biggest open questions?
d: The plug-density requirement, plug-magnet cyclic fatigue, and breeder confinement and divertor assumptions.

t: What can I do with Kronos's open data?
d: Download it, re-run it, verify the numbers, and cite it — it is CC BY 4.0.

t: What happens if something fails mid-operation?
d: The plasma simply cools and stops within seconds — there is no stored energy to run away.

t: What if the burner's plug requirement can't be met?
d: Then the burner does not close as a net-power machine — which is exactly why Kronos labels it requirement-class.

t: What does it mean that Kronos is a 'driven' system?
d: It is continuously heated rather than self-igniting — which makes it controllable.
A straight fusion machine plugged at both ends by high-field magnets and an electric potential.
Kronos's breeder — a compact spherical tokamak that makes neutrons, tritium and helium-3.

t: Why does neutron wall loading matter so much?
d: It sets how fast materials wear and how often components are replaced.

t: What is the plug-density ratio and why does it matter?
d: It is the burner's binding requirement — the plug must reach ~16× the central density to confine the plasma.

t: What is the single biggest technical risk?
d: The burner's plug-density requirement — the one item that most gates net electric power.

t: Kronos is a small company — why believe any of this?
d: Because you can download and re-run the engines, and every caveat is stated up front.

t: What Reproducibility Does and Doesn't Prove
d: Reproducing a computation proves it follows from the model and inputs — not that the unbuilt machine will behave that way.

t: What is the catch with the burner?
d: Net power is requirement-class: it depends on reaching a plug-density ratio near 16.
Kronos gives gate-based milestones, not a fixed date — and stages a saleable product ahead of net electricity.
A breeder-first, two-machine, openly-validated path — distinct from the single-D–T-tokamak mainstream.

t: Why build the breeder if electricity is not its product?
d: Because its products — tritium, neutrons, isotopes, helium-3 — have value independent of net-electric fusion.
A firm, clean, staged path to fusion value — argued in the open.

t: Why not just build one D–T machine like everyone else?
d: Because a breeder-plus-low-neutron-burner sells a product sooner and makes cleaner electricity.
High-temperature superconductors, modern computation and open validation have changed what a small team can credibly design.

t: Why should a national lab care about Kronos?
d: Because everything is reproducible, honestly graded, and anchored to the shared physics database.

t: Why a spherical tokamak for the breeder?
d: It holds more plasma pressure per tesla — the route to a compact neutron source.

t: Why does Kronos use two different fuels?
d: Because fuel should follow purpose: D–T to breed and make neutrons, D–³He to make clean electricity.

t: Why does Kronos build two different machines?
d: Because fuel should follow purpose: one machine breeds fuel, the other burns it for electricity.
